name: Parahippocampal gyrus
func: A ridge on the inner underside of the temporal lobe next to the hippocampus. It is the main gateway into the hippocampus, carrying information in for memory, and it is key for recognizing places and scenes.

levels.kid:
The **parahippocampal gyrus** is a long bump on the bottom of your brain, on the inside edge. "Para" means "next to," so its name means "the bump next to the hippocampus."

The hippocampus is your memory maker, and the parahippocampal gyrus is like the **front door** to it. Information about what you saw and did goes through this door to get stored as a memory.

It is really good at **places**. When you walk into your classroom and know right away where you are, this part of your brain is helping. It also helps you remember your way home.
levels.hs:
The **parahippocampal gyrus** is on the **inferior and medial surface of the temporal lobe**. It runs from front to back along the edge of the brain right next to the **midbrain**, sitting just below and beside the **hippocampus**, which is tucked into the floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. On its outer side, the **collateral sulcus** separates it from the fusiform gyrus. Behind, it joins the **isthmus of the cingulate gyrus**, completing the ring of the **limbic lobe**. At the front it curls back on itself to form the **uncus**, a hook-shaped bump that sits right next to the edge of the tentorium.

The front part of the gyrus contains the **entorhinal cortex**, the main input and output gateway of the hippocampus. Signals from all over the cortex funnel through the entorhinal cortex into the hippocampus, and memories flow back out the same way.

The back part is the **parahippocampal cortex**, which is specialized for **places and scenes**. It responds strongly when you look at a room, a street or a landscape, and it helps you find your way around.

Because of its position, the parahippocampal gyrus is important in **Alzheimer disease**, which damages the entorhinal cortex very early, and in **uncal herniation**, where swelling pushes the uncus against the brainstem.
levels.college:
The parahippocampal gyrus contains several regions with different cortex types:

- **Entorhinal cortex (BA 28 and part of 34)** in the anterior gyrus, including the surface of the uncus: a six-layered periallocortex marked by **verrucae**, tiny wart-like bumps on its surface produced by clusters of large layer II stellate and pyramidal cells.
- **Perirhinal cortex (BA 35, 36)** along the collateral sulcus: object recognition and familiarity.
- **Parahippocampal cortex (often called TF/TH in monkeys)** posteriorly: spatial and contextual information.
- **Presubiculum and parasubiculum** on the medial edge, next to the subiculum.

**Two information streams** enter the hippocampus. The **perirhinal cortex → lateral entorhinal cortex** route carries information about objects ("what"), and the **parahippocampal cortex → medial entorhinal cortex** route carries spatial and contextual information ("where"). These converge in the hippocampus to form memories binding items to contexts.

The entorhinal cortex sends the **perforant path** to the dentate gyrus and CA3 (from layer II) and the **temporoammonic path** to CA1 and the subiculum (from layer III). Output returns from CA1 and the subiculum to the deep layers (V and VI) and then to widespread cortex.

**Parahippocampal place area (PPA):** an fMRI region at the junction of the posterior parahippocampal gyrus and the lingual and fusiform gyri, responding more to scenes than to faces or objects (Epstein and Kanwisher 1998).

**Blood supply:** the **posterior cerebral artery** (anterior and posterior temporal branches) supplies most of the gyrus, with the **anterior choroidal artery** contributing to the uncus.
levels.phd:
**Grid cells:** in the medial entorhinal cortex, neurons fire at multiple locations forming a **hexagonal grid** across an environment (Hafting, Fyhn, Molden, Moser and Moser 2005). Grid spacing increases in discrete steps from the dorsal to the ventral entorhinal cortex, roughly by a constant ratio, creating modules that can encode position efficiently. Medial entorhinal cortex also contains **head-direction cells**, **border cells**, **speed cells** and **object-vector cells**. Grid-like signals have been found in humans with fMRI and intracranial recordings, even during imagined navigation and abstract "conceptual spaces."

**Lateral entorhinal cortex** neurons encode objects and their positions and carry signals that track the passage of time across experiences (Tsao and colleagues 2018), supporting the "what and when" of episodic memory.

**Layer II stellate cells** show **subthreshold membrane oscillations** at theta frequency and a strong hyperpolarization-activated current (I_h) whose gradient along the dorsoventral axis may help set grid scale.

**Perirhinal cortex** supports recognition of complex objects. Its neurons decrease firing when an object is seen again (**repetition suppression**), a candidate signal for familiarity. Dual-process models propose that perirhinal cortex supports **familiarity** while the hippocampus supports **recollection**, although this division is still debated.

**Vulnerability in Alzheimer disease:** in Braak staging, **tau neurofibrillary tangles** first appear in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, especially layer II neurons, before spreading to the hippocampus and neocortex. Loss of entorhinal layer II neurons is detectable even at the earliest stages of cognitive decline (Gómez-Isla 1996). Proposed reasons for this vulnerability include high metabolic demand, specific gene expression patterns and the trans-synaptic spread of tau along entorhinal-hippocampal pathways.
levels.expert:
**Uncal (transtentorial) herniation:** a mass in the temporal lobe or middle fossa, such as an **epidural hematoma** from a torn middle meningeal artery or a large subdural hematoma, pushes the uncus over the free edge of the **tentorium cerebelli**. Classic sequence:

1. **Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil** from compression of the **oculomotor nerve**, whose outer parasympathetic fibers are affected first.
2. Contralateral weakness, from compression of the cerebral peduncle.
3. In some patients, weakness on the *same* side as the lesion, because the opposite peduncle is pushed against the tentorial edge, the **Kernohan notch phenomenon**, a "false localizing sign."
4. Compression of the **posterior cerebral artery**, causing occipital infarction, then brainstem compression and decreased consciousness.

This is an emergency requiring rapid CT and often surgical decompression.

**Alzheimer disease:** MRI shows **medial temporal atrophy**, graded with the **Scheltens (MTA) scale** by the width of the choroidal fissure, temporal horn and hippocampal height. Entorhinal and parahippocampal atrophy and tau-PET signal appear early.

**Epilepsy:** in temporal lobe epilepsy, seizures may start in or spread through the entorhinal cortex. Smell or taste auras suggest involvement of the uncus ("uncinate fits").

**Topographical disorientation:** damage to the posterior parahippocampal gyrus, usually from a **PCA stroke**, especially on the right, causes **landmark agnosia**: patients cannot recognize familiar buildings or scenes and get lost in familiar places.

**Surgery:** during **amygdalohippocampectomy** or anterior temporal lobectomy for epilepsy, the parahippocampal gyrus and uncus are often removed with the hippocampus. Surgeons work carefully along the medial edge, the **pial bank**, to protect the oculomotor nerve, PCA, anterior choroidal artery and the brainstem, which lie just on the other side of the thin pia.

keyPoints: Inferomedial temporal lobe, beside the hippocampus and midbrain
Front end curls into the uncus
Entorhinal cortex = main gateway into and out of the hippocampus
Posterior part (PPA) is specialized for scenes and places
Grid cells in medial entorhinal cortex; earliest tau tangles in Alzheimer disease
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral dilated pupil (CN III)

test.q: Which sulcus separates the parahippocampal gyrus from the fusiform gyrus?
test.explain: The collateral sulcus runs along its lateral side.

test.q: The hook-shaped front end of the parahippocampal gyrus is called the ______.
test.explain: The uncus can herniate over the tentorium and compress CN III.

test.q: Which cortex in the anterior parahippocampal gyrus is the main gateway to the hippocampus?
test.explain: The entorhinal cortex sends the perforant path to the hippocampus.

test.q: Neurons in medial entorhinal cortex that fire in a hexagonal pattern across a room are:
test.explain: Grid cells were discovered by the Mosers (Nobel Prize 2014).

test.q: Weakness on the same side as a herniating mass, from the opposite peduncle hitting the tentorium, is called the Kernohan ______ phenomenon.
test.explain: It is a false localizing sign in uncal herniation.

test.q: Where do tau tangles appear first in Alzheimer disease, according to Braak staging?
test.explain: Braak stages I–II involve the transentorhinal and entorhinal regions.
